title: AI Writing Tool Procurement Checklist: Workflow, Risk, and Cost
description: A procurement checklist for AI writing tools: define acceptable use, test brand and factual quality, review privacy and ownership terms, validate integrations, and estimate full cost before rollout.

sections.title: Define the permitted use cases
sections.body: List the writing tasks the team wants to support, such as first drafts, summarizing approved material, rewriting for accessibility, product descriptions, or internal documentation. Separate low-risk drafting from work that needs verified facts, confidential inputs, legal review, or regulated claims. For each task, define what data may be entered, who reviews the output, and which decisions must remain with a person. Do not assume one provider is best for a category without testing the actual workflow.

sections.title: Create a repeatable evaluation set
sections.body: Build a small set of representative prompts from work the team is allowed to use for evaluation. Include a routine task, a difficult edge case, a style constraint, and an example where the right answer is to ask for missing information rather than invent it. Give every shortlisted tool the same instructions and source material. Score factual errors, omissions, tone, edit time, consistency, and how often the tool follows constraints. Keep the examples and scoring rubric so later model or product changes can be compared.

sections.title: Check factual quality and source handling
sections.body: Fluent prose is not evidence that a claim is correct. Verify names, dates, quotations, calculations, product capabilities, and citations against original sources. If a tool supplies references, open them and confirm that they support the exact statement. Record unsupported claims and the time required to correct them. For publishing workflows, decide which statements require primary-source review and whether an editor must approve every external-facing draft.

sections.title: Validate workflow and export requirements
sections.body: Map the tool into the actual drafting and approval process. Test permissions, shared workspaces, version history, review comments, templates, content-management integrations, API access, and exports using the intended plan. Check how it behaves when an integration fails and whether editors can recover previous versions. A long integration list is not proof that your exact workflow is supported; verify the required connection and permissions with current product documentation.

sections.title: Review privacy, retention, and access controls
sections.body: Before entering company material, review the provider's current terms for data retention, model training, subprocessors, deletion, data residency, access logging, and administrator controls. Distinguish consumer accounts from business or enterprise offerings because settings and contractual commitments may differ. Test role permissions and offboarding. Do not enter personal, customer, confidential, or regulated data until the organization has approved the provider and configuration for that data class.

sections.title: Check ownership, originality, and disclosure needs
sections.body: Do not assume that a vendor's content-ownership statement guarantees copyright protection, exclusivity, or that every output is original. Read the current contract, acceptable-use rules, and any indemnity limitations. Review outputs for accidental similarity, fabricated citations, trademark misuse, and unsupported claims; plagiarism or similarity detectors can help triage but are not legal clearance. Follow the disclosure and human-review policies relevant to your organization, customers, and jurisdiction.

sections.title: Compare full cost at expected usage
sections.body: Compare the exact plans required for your workflow, including seats, usage or credit limits, premium features, API charges, storage, integrations, support, taxes, and renewal terms. Estimate review and correction time as well as subscription fees. Model a normal month and a high-usage month, then verify overage behavior and cancellation/export options. Avoid relying on old headline prices or cost-per-word assumptions unless they match current plan limits and your measured workload.

sections.title: Procurement decision checklist
sections.body: Before rollout, confirm that the tool passed the same representative evaluation as alternatives; factual review responsibilities are documented; sensitive-data rules and retention terms are approved; roles and offboarding work; integrations and exports are tested on the intended plan; ownership and acceptable-use terms are understood; the full monthly and renewal costs are calculated; and a fallback exists if the provider changes pricing, limits, or model behavior. Start with a limited pilot and expand only when the team can demonstrate useful outcomes without unacceptable quality or risk.

author: Marcus Rivera
